options: Each row has a known answer (label) to learn from
The model trains itself with no data
questions.explain: Supervised = the data already has the answer (label y) the model learns to predict.

questions.q: Why do we split data into a training set and a test set?
options: To check the model on data it has NOT seen before
questions.explain: The test set is an honest exam: data the model never saw during training.
0.2 = 20% held out for testing; the rest (80%) is for training.

options: Makes the split the same every time (reproducible)
questions.explain: A fixed random_state makes the random split repeatable, so everyone gets the same result.

options: When test information sneaks into training and gives a fake-high score
When the model is too small
questions.explain: Leakage = the model secretly sees test info during training, so the score looks better than reality.

questions.q: When you scale features, you should fit the scaler on:
questions.explain: Fit on TRAIN only, then apply to test. Fitting on test data is cheating.

questions.q: Linear Regression is used to predict:
questions.explain: Linear Regression predicts a continuous number.

questions.q: Logistic Regression is mainly used for:
questions.explain: Despite its name, Logistic Regression does classification.

questions.q: How does a Decision Tree make a prediction?
options: By a chain of yes/no questions (splits)
By measuring distance to a center
questions.explain: A tree walks down yes/no questions until it reaches a leaf (the answer).

options: many decision trees that vote together
questions.explain: Random Forest = many trees; they vote (classification) or average (regression).
MAE = Mean Absolute Error — the average size of the mistakes.
RMSE squares the errors, so big mistakes hurt it more than MAE.

questions.q: If RMSE is much bigger than MAE, it usually means:
options: there are a few big mistakes (outliers)
questions.explain: A big gap between RMSE and MAE signals some large individual errors.
R² = 1 → perfect predictions. R² = 0 → no better than the average.

questions.q: An R² score of 0 means the model:
options: is no better than just predicting the average (a lazy baseline)
questions.explain: R² = 0 means the model performs like the always-predict-the-mean baseline.
Accuracy = how many predictions were correct out of all of them.

options: the classes are imbalanced (one is much rarer)
questions.explain: On imbalanced data, always predicting the majority class looks accurate but is useless.

options: How many real positives did we catch?
Of the ones we predicted positive, how many are truly positive?
questions.explain: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): how trustworthy the positive predictions are.

options: Of the truly positive cases, how many did we catch?
questions.explain: Recall = TP / (TP + FN): how many of the real positives we found.

options: the sum of precision and recall
a balance (harmonic mean) of precision and recall
questions.explain: F1 balances precision and recall; it drops toward the smaller of the two.

options: the data has NO labels — we find hidden groups ourselves
questions.explain: Unsupervised = no answer column; we discover structure (groups) on our own.

options: putting similar points into groups (with no answer key)
questions.explain: Clustering groups similar rows together when there are no labels.

options: a real data point picked at random
the average position of the points in a group
questions.explain: A center is the mean (average) position of its group — usually NOT a real data point.

questions.q: True or false: a K-Means center is always one of the real data points.
options: False — it is a made-up average point
questions.explain: The center is an invented average location, not necessarily any real point.

options: assign each point to the nearest center, move each center to the average, repeat
questions.explain: Assign → move → assign → move … until the centers stop moving.

options: the centers stop moving / points stop switching groups
questions.explain: Convergence = nothing changes anymore.

options: the number of groups K, before running
questions.explain: K-Means needs K up front (use the elbow/silhouette to choose it).

options: runs 10 times from different random starts and keeps the best
questions.explain: K-Means depends on the starting spot, so it tries 10 starts and keeps the tightest result.

questions.q: Why must you scale features before K-Means?
options: because it uses distance, so a big-number column would dominate
questions.explain: K-Means measures distance; without scaling, large-range features drown out small ones.

options: how tight the groups are (total distance from points to their center)
questions.explain: Lower inertia = tighter groups. More clusters always lowers it.

options: choose K by finding the 'bend' in the inertia-vs-K plot
questions.explain: Plot inertia vs K and pick the K where adding more groups stops helping much.

options: how well each point fits its group (higher = better)
questions.explain: Silhouette (−1 to 1) measures fit; higher average means cleaner clusters.

options: starting with each point alone and repeatedly merging the two closest groups
questions.explain: Bottom-up: every point starts alone, then the closest groups keep merging into a tree.

questions.q: In hierarchical clustering, you choose the number of groups by:
options: cutting the dendrogram (tree) at a chosen height — after seeing it
questions.explain: You don't pick K up front; you cut the tree where you like.

questions.q: On a dendrogram, cutting LOWER (near the points) gives you:
questions.explain: Cut low = many small groups; cut high = few big groups.

options: the rule for measuring distance between two GROUPS
questions.explain: Linkage = how you measure group-to-group distance (single, complete, average, ward).

questions.q: Which linkage is the usual safe default for round blob-shaped groups?
questions.explain: Ward (keeps groups tightest) is the common default for round, separated blobs.

options: follow long chains / curvy shapes (like moons)
questions.explain: Single linkage uses the closest pair, so it chains along curves.

questions.q: The main limitation of hierarchical clustering is:
options: it is slow on big data (compares everyone to everyone)
questions.explain: It scales poorly — fine under ~10,000 points, painful beyond.

options: density — wherever points are packed tightly together
questions.explain: DBSCAN finds dense 'crowds'; that's why it handles any shape.
